newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Rwanda genocide tribunal faces new postponement.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda genocide tribunal faces new postponement.

text.p: The International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda faced a second delay in 24 hours on Thursday as a defence lawyer said he would quit unless he won a postponement.
Tribunal officials said defendant Jean Paul Akayesu would arrive at court on Thursday for what should be the first trial of any Rwandan accused of genocide and crimes against humanity in 1994.

But Johan Scheers, Belgian defence lawyer for the 43-year-old Hutu, told reporters he would resign and go home unless he won a preliminary motion for a postponement because he had not been given enough time to prepare a defence case.
"He tells me he is innocent. It is impossible at this moment to say whether he is innocent," Scheers said on Wednesday.
Lawyers said if Scheers fulfilled his vow to resign unless he won a delay, then another defence lawyer would have to be appointed and doubtless would also ask for a new postponement.

Akayesu was bourgmestre, or local government leader, in Rwanda's Taba commune in the three-month genocide and is charged with failing to stop killings, inciting the public to slaughter, hunting down minority Tutsis and ordering killings.

The three-judge tribunal, ordered by the United Nations in November 1994 to bring leaders of the genocide to justice, on Wednesday postponed the trial of another Rwandan Hutu on the grounds of sickness.

The tribunal has been dogged by delays, poor communications from its base in this northern Tanzanian farming town and the vast problem of finding who was responsible for a genocide that nearly achieved its aims of wiping out an entire ethnic group.
It has indicted only 21 suspects and holds only three in detention, charged with crimes against humanity and genocide.
Scheers said he received prosecution documents in late July and up to a third of their testimony was blacked out to protect witnesses, leaving him in the dark about his defence.
Asked what he would do if the court decided Akayesu's trial should go ahead as scheduled on Thursday, having already been once postponed, Scheers said: "I would leave. I would resign."
"I will ask for a delay. I will try to find a new way of working with the tribunal," said Scheers, adding he wanted to explain to the court the problem of finding defence witnesses.
He said he had twice visited camps in east Zaire, unhappy host to an estimated 1.1 million Rwandan Hutu refugees, searching for up to 40 defence witnesses named by Akayesu.
"I have three members of the family in Belgium who can say he is a very nice man," said Scheers, adding that the three, like many would-be witnesses, were afraid of coming to Arusha.
He said it was essential to meet defence witnesses in the refugee camps in Zaire but Zairean authorities were preventing the refugee lobby groups who might find them from operating.

"The prosecution has investigated for 18 months and has only 20 witnesses -- either they are working very slowly or they are not revealing all of them," said Scheers, adding that the prosecution said 85 witnesses had been killed since January.

On Wednesday, the tribunal court agreed to a postponement in the trial of Georges Rutaganda but refused a defence request for his release. His Belgian defence lawyer said unless he received treatment elsewhere he would die before the trial. He declined to reveal the nature of Rutaganda's illness.
The tribunal's mandate is to try top genocide planners and perpetrators, not the tens of thousands of ordinary killers.
